nameStory: The red-headed ash borer gets its name from two key features that make it easy to remember: its distinctive reddish-orange head and its larval lifestyle of boring tunnels through ash trees. This beetle is a classic example of a common name that tells you exactly what to look for and where to find it!
description: The red-headed ash borer is a medium-sized longhorn beetle with a striking appearance that makes it stand out from other wood-boring insects. Adults typically measure about half an inch long and sport a bright reddish-orange head and thorax that contrasts beautifully with their dark wing covers. Like all longhorn beetles, they have notably long antennae that can be nearly as long as their body. You'll most often spot these active beetles crawling on or flying around ash trees during warm months.

idTips.label: Reddish-orange head
idTips.description: The head and front section (thorax) are bright reddish-orange to rusty red, creating a striking contrast that's visible from several feet away

idTips.label: Dark wing covers
idTips.description: The hard wing covers (elytra) are dark brown to black, often with a slight metallic sheen when caught in sunlight

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae extend well beyond the body length, feeling rigid and segmented if you gently touch them, typical of longhorn beetles

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About half an inch long, roughly the size of your thumbnail, with a somewhat elongated, cylindrical body shape

idTips.label: Ash tree association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near ash trees, often crawling on bark that may smell faintly sweet from tree sap

habitat: Look for red-headed ash borers wherever ash trees grow throughout New England's forests, parks, and suburban areas. They're particularly common in mixed hardwood forests at low to moderate elevations, especially in areas with white ash, green ash, or black ash trees. You might also spot them in urban settings where ash trees are planted as street trees or in landscaped areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from ash trees in late spring as temperatures warm, often seen crawling on sunny bark surfaces or taking short flights between trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively mating and laying eggs in ash bark crevices. This is your best time to spot them.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases as they complete their reproductive cycle, though you may still find a few stragglers on warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae are developing inside ash trees, creating tiny sawdust piles at the base of infested trees.

funFact: Despite being called an ash borer, the red-headed ash borer actually prefers dead or dying ash trees over healthy ones, making it more of a cleanup crew than a tree killer - unlike the devastating emerald ash borer that attacks healthy trees!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse this native beetle with the invasive emerald ash borer, which is metallic green and much more destructive. Remember: red head = native friend, green body = invasive enemy. The red-headed ash borer is also much larger and more colorful than most other wood-boring beetles you'll encounter.
contextualKnowledge: With ash trees under severe threat from the invasive emerald ash borer, native species like the red-headed ash borer are losing their habitat across New England. Ironically, this native ash specialist is being displaced by its foreign cousin that's killing ash forests region-wide.
compareHints: As the only Neoclytus species commonly found in New England, the red-headed ash borer stands apart from other longhorn beetles by its distinctive two-toned coloration. Most other longhorn beetles in the region are either uniformly dark or have different color patterns, and few show such a clear contrast between a bright reddish front end and dark wing covers.
